findings.title: Domain-form tenant id is accepted by the config screen but can never sign in (tid check compares a GUID to the domain)
findings.rationale: `AppState::new` passes the configured tenant string straight into `EntraAuthService::new` (state.rs:258) and nothing resolves a domain to its GUID (grep: no openid-configuration lookup outside `commands/sso`). The `tid` claim is always the tenant GUID, so with `tenant_id = "contoso.onmicrosoft.com"` (which `set_auth_config` validates and saves, message: "Directory (tenant) ID must be a GUID or a tenant domain") the exchange succeeds at Entra and then fails locally with `token_exchange`, whose sign-in hint tells the operator to "verify the app's client and tenant IDs". `UserSettings::remembered_account_for(&self.tenant_id)` (settings.rs:162-165) compares the GUID from the claims to the domain too, so even if sign-in were relaxed, launch restore would be refused every time. A configuration path the UI advertises is unusable end to end.
findings.proposal: Resolve a non-GUID tenant once to its GUID and use that as the effective `tenant_id`: either at `AppState::new` via `{auth_root}/{tenant}/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration` (the repo already does this discovery in `commands/sso/mod.rs:101`; the `issuer` carries the GUID), or lazily in `sign_in` (accept when `self.tenant_id` is not a GUID, then store the resolved GUID for `remembered_account_for` and the keyring key). Add a `sign_in`-level test with a mock `/token` returning a GUID `tid` against a domain-configured service (needs finding on browser-opener injection), and a `settings.rs` test that a domain-configured tenant restores. Alternatively drop domain support from `is_valid_tenant` and say so in the first-run UI; today the two disagree.
findings.verifier_notes: Evidence real. service/mod.rs:313-318 compares the id-token `tid` (always the tenant GUID) to `self.tenant_id` verbatim; state.rs:258 passes the resolved string straight into `EntraAuthService::new`; no openid-configuration discovery exists outside `commands/sso/mod.rs:101` (used only to build output URLs, not to resolve the configured tenant). config.rs:41-46,71-73 accepts a dotted domain and the UI advertises it (web-rs/views/config_screen.rs:125 placeholder 'GUID or contoso.onmicrosoft.com', :177 hint). `UserSettings::remembered_account_for` (settings.rs:162-166) filters on `account.tenant_id == tenant_id`, so even a relaxed sign-in would never restore. No doc, CHANGELOG or test claims domain support works end to end (settings.rs:277 only round-trips the string). Deterministic failure of an advertised config path with a misleading `token_exchange` hint ('verify the app's client and tenant IDs') justifies high; the cheapest fix is to reject domains in `is_valid_tenant` and update config_screen.rs copy.
findings.recheck_notes: Refutation attempted and failed; the failing path is fully constructible in the shipped build. (1) Entry: apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/config.rs:41-46,71-73 — `set_auth_config` accepts any dotted whitespace-free string via `is_valid_tenant` and persists it to settings.json; the frontend advertises it (apps/desktop/web-rs/src/views/config_screen.rs:125 placeholder "GUID or contoso.onmicrosoft.com", :176-177 "must be a GUID or a domain like contoso.onmicrosoft.com"). (2) No normalization anywhere: apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/state.rs:128-146 `resolve` returns the raw string; state.rs:241-258 passes it verbatim to `EntraAuthService::new`, which stores it unchanged (crates/azapptoolkit-auth/src/service/mod.rs:83-87). `grep openid-configuration` across the repo finds no discovery fetch; the only hit is commands/sso/mod.rs:100-104 `oidc_summary_urls`, a static string formatter for the SSO summary panel, not a lookup (so the proposal's "repo already does this discovery" is inaccurate, though the fix direction stands). (3) The authority `{auth_root}/contoso.onmicrosoft.com` (service/mod.rs:219) is valid for Entra, so /authorize + /token succeed and the id_token `tid` claim is the tenant GUID (Entra always emits tid as a GUID). service/mod.rs:313-318 then does an exact `tenant_id != self.tenant_id` string compare with no non-GUID branch and returns `AuthError::TokenExchange`, which the sign-in view maps to the generic `token_exchange` hint (sign_in.rs:164) that misleads the operator toward the client/tenant IDs. (4) Launch restore is independently blocked: crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/settings.rs:162-166 `remembered_account_for` filters `account.tenant_id == tenant_id` (GUID from claims vs configured domain), called from state.rs:377. (5) No repo_invariants test or auth unit test covers a domain-form tenant (the only `tid` mismatch string exists at service/mod.rs:315; no test asserts it), and docs/DEVELOPMENT.md:52,72 and README.md:401 document only GUIDs — the domain path was added to the config screen without ever being wired through. Severity stays high: an advertised, validated configuration path is 100% unusable end to end and the resulting error hint points at the wrong cause; only the GUID path works. Not a security exposure (the check fails closed), purely a correctness/UX bug.

findings.title: sign_out clears in-memory session before the fallible keyring delete; on failure the restore pointer, data caches and refresh token survive while the UI reports 'still signed in'
findings.rationale: If `delete_refresh_token` errors (locked Secret Service, Credential Manager hiccup, `ensure_keyring_store` failure), `sign_out` returns `Err` after `known_tenants` and the token cache were already cleared, and the command returns before `forget_account()` and `state.cache.invalidate_tenant(...)`. Result: (a) every subsequent command fails `not_signed_in` while the shell stays mounted and the toast says "you are still signed in" — false; (b) `settings.json.last_account` and the keyring refresh token both survive, so the NEXT launch `restore_session` revives the exact session the operator just tried to end — the fail-open direction on a shared workstation; (c) the tenant's data caches (`state.cache`) are not swept, contradicting the comment that sign-out "must" drop every tenant-scoped entry. The doc on `forget_account` says the two must not disagree about whether anyone is signed in; this path makes them disagree.
findings.proposal: Make sign-out fail-safe: in `EntraAuthService::sign_out` attempt `delete_refresh_token` FIRST (via `spawn_blocking`, see the inline-keyring finding) and only then clear `cache`/`known_tenants`; in the command, run `forget_account()`, client removal and `state.cache.invalidate_tenant` unconditionally (before or regardless of the keyring result) and return the keyring error afterwards so the toast can say precisely "signed out, but the OS credential store still holds a token — remove the azapptoolkit entry manually". Update the shell.rs message accordingly. Add a service test with a keyring store that fails `delete_credential` (a small `keyring_core::CredentialStoreApi` fake) asserting `known_tenants` is empty AND the error is returned.
findings.verifier_notes: Evidence real: service/mod.rs:561-566 invalidates the token cache and removes `known_tenants` BEFORE `delete_refresh_token(..)?`; commands/auth.rs:49 returns on Err before `forget_account()` (:53) and `state.cache.invalidate_tenant` (:61); shell.rs:82-85 tells the operator they are still signed in although every later command now fails `not_signed_in`. No repo_invariants test covers sign_out ordering. Downgraded from high: it needs a keyring failure at exactly that moment, the UI does tell the operator sign-out failed, and a retry re-runs the (idempotent) path; the fail-open next-launch restore only happens if the keyring later recovers. Still a real ordering bug worth the proposed fix (delete first, or clear pointer/caches unconditionally and report the keyring error afterwards).

findings.title: CAE-ness is not part of the token cache key, and every interactive/restore flow seeds the Graph slots with non-CAE tokens — violating the invariant state.rs documents
findings.rationale: `graph_for` (state.rs:417-464) builds every Graph adapter with `ScopedTokenAdapter::new_cae`, i.e. it expects `cp1`-advertised tokens in the `(tenant, scope_key)` slot. But `sign_in` (mod.rs:332), `consent_for_scopes` (381-388), `reauthenticate` (661-669), `refresh_session` (583) and `restore_session` (617) all put a token minted WITHOUT the `claims` parameter into those same slots. `authorize_url` (114-152) also sends no `claims`. So after launch (restore), after "Refresh Token", after every "Grant consent", and after reauth the Graph read/write adapters serve a non-CAE token for up to its full lifetime — exactly the class of bug the state.rs comment forbids for the `ensure_*` probes and that `readiness.rs:272-291` goes out of its way to avoid. CAE tokens are the ones that revoke promptly on password reset / disabled user / risky sign-in, which is the security property the app opted into.
findings.proposal: Make it structural: include CAE-ness in the cache key (`TokenCache::get/put` take a `cae: bool` folded into `scope_key`, or a `CacheSlot { scopes, cae }`), so a non-CAE seed can never be served to a `new_cae` adapter — the worst case becomes one extra silent refresh. Then have the five flows mint CAE for Graph audiences: pass `claims = build_cae_claims(None)` on the `/authorize` and `/token` requests in `run_auth_code_flow` when the scope set is a Graph one, and use `access_token_for_scopes_cae(.., None)` in `refresh_session`/`restore_session`. Add a wiremock test asserting the `claims` form field is present on the refresh for a Graph scope set and that `cache.get(tenant, read_scopes, cae=true)` is what `graph_for` consumes.
findings.verifier_notes: Evidence real. token_cache.rs:120-146 keys the cache by `(tenant_id, scope_key)` only; state.rs:417-469 builds every Graph adapter with `new_cae`, whose `bearer()` (token_adapter.rs:71-74) calls `access_token_for_scopes_cae(.., None)` → `access_token_inner` (mod.rs:478-483) returns whatever is in the slot. `sign_in` (mod.rs:332), `consent_for_scopes` (:381-388), `reauthenticate` (:661-668), `refresh_session` (:583) and `restore_session` (:617) all seed Graph scope slots with tokens minted without `claims` (`run_auth_code_flow` params :282-289 carry no `claims`; `authorize_url` :114-152 none either). state.rs:563-565 documents the invariant these flows violate; readiness.rs:277-283 honours it. No doc/CHANGELOG records this as deliberate (only CHANGELOG-archive.md:2530 mentions the CAE pairing). Impact is a lost security property (prompt revocation) for one token lifetime after each of those flows, not a functional break — medium is honest.

findings.title: `interaction_required` / `login_required` are classified as a dead refresh token and purge the whole session; MSAL treats them as a per-resource step-up with the RT still valid
findings.rationale: AADSTS50076/50079/50158 (MFA / registration / external challenge required by Conditional Access for THIS resource) come back from a `refresh_token` grant as `error: "interaction_required"`; AADSTS50074 similarly. The refresh token remains fully valid for other audiences — MSAL surfaces `InteractionRequiredAuthError` and re-acquires interactively for that resource without discarding the account. Here a first ARM/Exchange/Log Analytics call under a "Require MFA for Azure management" or authentication-strength policy deletes the keyring token, drops every cached access token and forgets the tenant, so Graph browsing dies too and the operator gets the `Re-authenticate` (`prompt=login`) toast. In the per-resource authentication-strength case the reauth mints only the Graph read token, the next ARM refresh fails again, and the purge repeats — a loop. The frontend's own hint table already treats these codes as "complete the MFA prompt", not "session dead", so the two layers disagree. error.rs:11-16 states the RT "must be discarded" for `interaction_required`; that premise is what this finding challenges.
findings.proposal: Add `AuthError::InteractionRequired(String)` (UI code `interaction_required`, not in `REAUTH_FATAL_CODES`, `retryable=false`) for `interaction_required`/`login_required` and for `invalid_grant` whose AADSTS is 50074/50076/50079/50158; do NOT purge in `access_token_inner` for it (mirror the `ConsentRequired` arm). Recover with a scope-targeted interactive round trip: generalise `consent_for_scopes` into `interactive_for_scopes(tenant, scopes, prompt)` and expose a `request_scope_step_up(tenant_id, feature)` command (or reuse `request_scope_consent` with `prompt=login`), and teach `Session::report_command_error` to offer "Verify identity" on that code. Pin with wiremock tests: `interaction_required` keeps the keyring token and `known_tenants`; 70008 still purges.
findings.verifier_notes: Evidence real: wire.rs:55-60 maps `interaction_required`/`login_required` to `InvalidGrant`, and mod.rs:529-538 purges the keyring token, all cached access tokens and the `known_tenants` entry. error.rs:14-16 documents the current stance ('must be discarded'), but Microsoft's own definition (MsalError.InteractionRequired: 'the application needs to expose the UI to the user so the user can do an interactive log-in to get a token with updated claims'; MSAL mitigation is AcquireTokenInteractive, the account is kept) contradicts it — the refresh token stays valid for other audiences. So a first ARM/Exchange/Log Analytics call under a resource-scoped MFA/authentication-strength CA policy kills Graph browsing too. The loop claim is real only when the policy is scoped to the non-Graph resource (a Graph `prompt=login` then does not satisfy it); with tenant-wide MFA one `reauthenticate` clears it — so the rationale slightly overstates frequency. sign_in.rs:225-228 already treats 50076/50079/50158 as 'complete MFA', confirming the layers disagree. Proposal (typed `InteractionRequired`, scope-targeted interactive step-up, no purge) is consistent with the existing `ConsentRequired` arm.

findings.title: Loopback honours an `error=` redirect before validating `state`, and writes the success page before the state check
findings.rationale: RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1 requires the error redirect to echo `state`, but the listener returns `Authorization(err)` on any request carrying `error=` without checking it. Any local process, or any web page open in the operator's browser (a cross-origin `fetch("http://127.0.0.1:<port>/?error=...")` still reaches the socket even though the response is opaque), can abort an in-flight sign-in and place an attacker-chosen string into the sign-in card (`"Sign-in failed: authorization request failed: {err}"`). The port is ephemeral but the range is small enough to spray. Separately, the browser tab is told "sign-in complete" even when `state` mismatches and the app is about to report `state_mismatch` — the page and the app disagree. `error_description` is also dropped, so the AADSTS code (65004 user-declined vs 53003 CA block) never reaches `aadsts_hint`.
findings.proposal: Reorder: parse `state` first; if it is absent or mismatched, respond 400 with a neutral page and `continue` the accept loop (a forged request should not end the wait) rather than returning; only after `state` matches branch on `error`/`code`. Whitelist the surfaced `error` value (known OAuth codes) and carry `extract_aadsts_code(error_description)` into the message via `redacted_aad_error`-style formatting so the existing hint table fires. Extend `state_mismatch_is_rejected` to assert the forged request does not terminate the listener and that a later valid redirect still succeeds.
findings.verifier_notes: Evidence real: loopback.rs:96-97 writes the 200 page, :99-101 returns `Authorization(err)` on any `error=` before the `state` check at :103-106, and `error_description` is never read (:65-72). The listener also ignores the HTTP method (:58 `let _method`), so even a CORS/PNA preflight `OPTIONS /?error=..` from a web page would terminate the wait. `state_mismatch_is_rejected` (:200-212) pins the current return-on-mismatch behaviour and would need updating as the proposal says. Message injection is text-only (Leptos renders text), so low is right; the proposal (validate `state` first, `continue` on forgery, carry the AADSTS code) is sound.

findings.title: `consent_required` is flattened to `token_error` inside every client call, so the shared UI consent fallback never fires for scoped calls; docs still blame a `String` boundary that no longer exists
findings.rationale: `token_adapter::token_error` (token_adapter.rs:21-29) now carries `consent_required` across the boundary as `TokenError { code: "consent_required", .. }`, but `ui_code()` only passes the two re-auth-fatal codes through and collapses everything else to `token_error`. So a Graph write/sharepoint/policy call that hits a missing consent still reaches the UI as `token_error`, and `Session::report_consent_required` (web-rs/state/errors.rs:112-117, keyed on `e.code == "consent_required"`) — described in the doc as "one shared fallback" for commands with no bespoke button — cannot fire. The `ensure_*` pre-acquisitions remain necessary only because of this second flattening, yet the doc, `.claude/rules/auth.md:18` and five `state.rs` comments (558, 617, 627, 655, …) attribute it to a `String` boundary that was removed. `consent_required` is already asserted non-fatal (reauth.rs:263) and non-retryable, so passing it through is safe for fan-outs (bulk.rs:1190-1197 treats it as per-item).
findings.proposal: Introduce `core::reauth::PASSTHROUGH_CODES = REAUTH_FATAL_CODES ∪ {"consent_required"}` (or make `passthrough_code` return `Some` for any non-empty classified `TokenError.code` and let `is_reauth_fatal` stay separate) so `GraphError/ArmError/ExchangeError/KeyVaultError::ui_code()` emit `consent_required`. Then rewrite the doc paragraph, `.claude/rules/auth.md`, and the `state.rs` comments to the true statement: the `ensure_*` probes exist to surface consent BEFORE side-effecting work and to bind a specific `consent_feature`, not because the boundary loses the code. Add a dto test: `UiError::from(GraphError::Token(TokenError::new("consent_required", ..))).code == "consent_required"`.
findings.verifier_notes: Evidence real: http_error.rs macro `ui_code` passes only `reauth::passthrough_code` results (reauth.rs:47-49 = REAUTH_FATAL_CODES), so `GraphError::Token(TokenError{code:'consent_required'})` → `token_error`, while token_adapter.rs:25 does carry `consent_required`. Stronger than stated: there is no `ensure_write_token` (state.rs:587-678 lists arm/policy_write/sharepoint/group_member/audit_log/exchange/log_analytics only), so the default `consent_feature = "write"` fallback documented in auth-and-consent.md:73-80 and use_command.rs:100 cannot fire for the very case it describes (first Graph write in an un-consented tenant). Docs are stale in part: auth-and-consent.md:82-83, .claude/rules/auth.md and state.rs:589-590/:601 blame a `String` boundary that `TokenError{code}` replaced; state.rs:558/617/628/656 ('generic token_error') remain accurate. Passing `consent_required` through is safe: `is_retryable_code` (http_retry.rs:25-27) excludes it, reauth.rs:74 asserts it non-fatal, bulk.rs:1187-1200 treats it per-item.

findings.title: Token endpoint calls have no retry/backoff; the readiness probe fans out six refreshes at once and a 429/5xx surfaces as a terminal `token_exchange`
findings.rationale: AGENTS.md makes `core::http_retry` the one retry budget ("incl. `$batch`"), and every REST client honours `Retry-After`, but the `/token` POST is a single attempt: a 429 from `login.microsoftonline.com` (which does throttle per client/tenant and returns `Retry-After`) or a transient 5xx/network error becomes `TokenExchange("HTTP 429")` → UI `token_exchange` (retryable=true but nothing retries), readiness shows `Unknown` for that half, and a `ScopedTokenAdapter::bearer()` failure aborts the Graph request that needed it. The readiness checklist and the per-audience refresh locks (token_cache.rs:226-229: "Access Readiness fans about six out at once") make simultaneous token requests the normal case, not an edge.
findings.proposal: Wrap the send in `azapptoolkit_core::http_retry::with_retries("aad_token", RetryClass::<idempotent>, |_| async { .. })`, classifying 429 (`Retry-After`), 5xx and `reqwest` transport errors as `Attempt::Retry` and everything else as `Done`. A `refresh_token` grant is idempotent (Entra does not revoke on use), so retrying is safe; an `authorization_code` exchange is single-use, so restrict retries there to transport errors before a response was received. Add a wiremock test: first 429 with `Retry-After: 1`, then 200 → token cached, exactly two requests.
findings.verifier_notes: Evidence real: mod.rs:154-202 is a single `send()`; no `retry` anywhere in the auth crate; `http_retry::is_retryable_code` covers only throttled/server_error/network_error, and graph transport.rs:495-498 fetches the bearer ONCE outside `with_retries` ('A 401 is non-retryable and surfaces to the caller'), so a client's retry budget never covers a transient token failure. readiness.rs:62-66 fans probes out concurrently as described. Concrete cost beyond readiness: `restore_session` at launch on a transient network blip → `Ok(None)` (commands/auth.rs:39-43) → the operator must redo the full browser sign-in although the keyring token is fine. The proposal's split (retry refresh_token grants; only transport errors for the single-use authorization_code exchange) is correct.

findings.title: On Linux without a Secret Service the sign-in hard-fails after the browser round trip; the requirement is undocumented and the `keyring` hint is misleading
findings.rationale: On Linux the only store is the D-Bus Secret Service; on a box without a session bus or `gnome-keyring`/`kwallet` (SSH + X forwarding, WSLg, minimal WMs, some containers) `Store::new()` fails, `ensure_keyring_store` memoises the failure forever (token_cache.rs:26-42), and `store_token_outcome` discards a perfectly good access token and returns `Keyring` — AFTER the operator completed the browser sign-in. The hint ("unlock ... then retry") cannot be followed because there is nothing to unlock, and every retry repeats the browser round trip. Nothing in README/DEVELOPMENT documents Secret Service as a hard requirement (README:326 still says "libsecret").
findings.proposal: At minimum: document the Linux Secret Service (zbus) requirement in README/DEVELOPMENT (README.md:326 still says libsecret), and make `ensure_keyring_store` failures distinguishable from a locked store so sign_in.rs:156-158 can say 'no credential store available' instead of 'unlock your keychain'. The in-memory refresh-token fallback is a product/security decision for the team (access tokens are already memory-only, so a session-only mode is defensible), not an obvious fix; if adopted, surface a `keyring_unavailable` notice as proposed.
findings.verifier_notes: Premise verified: token_cache.rs:26-42 memoises the store-registration failure in a `OnceLock`; :65-69 the only Linux store is `zbus_secret_service_keyring_store`; mod.rs:455-459 fails `store_token_outcome` after a successful code exchange; sign_in.rs:156-158 tells the operator to 'unlock' something that does not exist. No doc states the hard requirement (only release-updater-demo.md:160-185 discusses the dependency graph). The proposal's in-memory fallback is a design change the finding presents as the fix; documentation + a precise hint is the uncontroversial part.

findings.title: `AuthError::Cancelled` is never constructed; the two real cancel paths (300 s timeout, `access_denied`) surface as `loopback`/`authorization` with misleading hints
findings.rationale: grep shows `AuthError::Cancelled` appears only in error.rs and the dto mapping — dead on the backend — while the frontend keeps a hint for the `cancelled` code that can never be reached. Meanwhile the two ways an operator actually cancels (closing the tab → 300 s later `Loopback("timed out…")` → code `loopback` → "Check your network and try again"; clicking Cancel on the consent screen → `error=access_denied` → `Authorization("access_denied")` → "The sign-in was declined. An administrator may need to grant the app consent") both produce the wrong advice. `dispatch`/DR already use a `cancelled` code meaningfully (dr.rs:81), so the vocabulary exists.
findings.proposal: Map the loopback timeout to `AuthError::Cancelled` (or a dedicated `Timeout` with its own code and hint), and map an `error=access_denied` redirect whose `error_description` carries no AADSTS code to `Cancelled` as well; keep `Authorization` for everything else and carry the AADSTS code through (see the loopback finding). Update the `From<AuthError> for UiError` test table (already lists `Cancelled`) and add a loopback test for the `error=` arm. Remove the variant instead if the team prefers the current codes — but then delete the frontend hint too.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: `AuthError::Cancelled` is constructed nowhere in the backend (only error.rs:42 and the dto mapping/test at dto/lib.rs:167,226); the loopback timeout maps to `Loopback(..)` (mod.rs:273-278 → UI code `loopback` → default 'Check your network' hint, sign_in.rs:169) and a consent-screen Cancel arrives as `Authorization("access_denied")` → 'The sign-in was declined. An administrator may need to grant the app consent' (sign_in.rs:160-163). Minor citation error: there is no `commands/dr.rs`; the `cancelled` code lives in audit.rs:334/1626. Otherwise accurate; low.

findings.title: Browser launch failure is only logged; the authorize URL is never surfaced, so the operator waits out the full 300 s with no way to proceed
findings.rationale: The warning says "user must open URL manually", but the full URL (with `state`, `code_challenge`) is — correctly — not logged anywhere and is not returned to the UI, so there is nothing for the user to open. On a desktop with no default browser handler, a snap/flatpak-confined `xdg-open`, or a Windows policy that blocks the handler, sign-in silently hangs until the 300 s timeout and then shows a network hint. grep of web-rs finds no "copy link"/manual-open affordance.
findings.proposal: Emit the authorize URL to the webview when the launcher fails: have `run_auth_code_flow` take an `on_open_failed: impl Fn(&Url)` callback (or return `AuthError::BrowserLaunch(url)` early while keeping the listener alive in a spawned task), and in `commands::auth::sign_in` forward it via a Tauri event so the sign-in card can render a "Couldn't open your browser — copy this link" button. The URL is single-use and bound by PKCE/state, so exposing it to the operator's own webview is safe. Also lowers the timeout's cost by giving a visible next step.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: mod.rs:263-268 only logs on `open_system_browser` failure and then waits on the 300 s timeout (:273-278); the URL is stripped from the log (:252-253) and never returned; no 'copy link'/manual-open affordance exists in web-rs (grep for copy link/open manually/browser_launch returns nothing). Enhancement, low.

findings.title: No test proves the single-flight refresh: N concurrent requests for one scope set should produce exactly one /token POST
findings.rationale: The struct doc (mod.rs:71-76) promises "same-key concurrency still collapses to one network call via the double-checked cache read taken under the lock", and the token_cache doc leans on it for keyring write safety, but the only test (`refresh_locks_are_keyed_per_tenant_and_scope_set`, 749-761) checks lock identity, not behaviour. A future edit that moves the second cache check, or makes `bypass_cache` sticky, would silently turn every Graph page walk into a refresh storm (each `bearer()` call hits this path) and multiply keyring writes — the exact splice hazard the chunk lock was added for.
findings.proposal: Add `#[tokio::test] concurrent_same_scope_requests_collapse_to_one_token_call`: mount the success mock with `.expect(1)`, seed `signed_in_service`, `join_all` eight `access_token_for_scopes` futures for the same scopes, assert all eight return the same token string and `server.verify()` passes; add a sibling asserting two DIFFERENT scope sets produce two POSTs (proves the per-key locks do not serialise unrelated audiences). Also cover `access_token_for_scopes_cae(.., Some(challenge))` bypassing the cache and sending a `claims` form field (wiremock `body_string_contains("claims=")`).
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: the only lock test is `refresh_locks_are_keyed_per_tenant_and_scope_set` (mod.rs:749-761), which checks `Arc::ptr_eq`, not that N concurrent callers produce one POST; no test uses `.expect(1)` or asserts a `claims=` form field on the CAE path. The wiremock harness (`signed_in_service`, `mount_token_success`) makes the proposed tests cheap. Downgraded to low: a regression would cost extra token round trips, and the keyring splice hazard the rationale leans on is already closed structurally by `CHUNK_SET_LOCK` + the chunk-count marker (token_cache.rs:175-187, 239-248).

findings.title: The interactive flow is untestable (hard-wired browser launch + internal listener), so sign_in's tid check, the nonce check, consent identity rejection and reauthenticate have no end-to-end test
findings.rationale: Because `open_system_browser` is called unconditionally and the redirect port is private to the function, no test can drive `sign_in`, `consent_for_scopes` or `reauthenticate`: the test module covers `ensure_same_identity` in isolation (1027-1061), `authorize_url` shape, and the silent paths only. Untested security-relevant branches: `id_token nonce mismatch` (294-296), `id token tid … does not match configured tenant` (313-318), `id token missing tid/oid` (306-321), the `consent`/`re-authentication` mismatch wiring (376, 660), `store_token_outcome` with `scope_fallback = &[]` at sign-in, and that `reauthenticate` re-inserts `known_tenants` only after validation. The wiremock harness already exists; only the seam is missing.
findings.proposal: Inject the launcher: add a `browser: Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> Result<()> + Send + Sync>` (default `open_system_browser`) to `EntraAuthService` with a `with_browser_opener` constructor for tests. A test opener parses the URL, extracts `redirect_uri`/`state`/`nonce`, and spawns a task that connects to the loopback port with `GET /?code=…&state=…`; the wiremock `/token` returns an id_token built with `URL_SAFE_NO_PAD` carrying the chosen `tid`/`oid`/`nonce`. Then add tests for: happy sign-in caches under read scopes; wrong `tid` rejected; nonce mismatch rejected; consent completed as a different `oid` rejected and cache untouched; reauth restores `known_tenants`. This also unlocks the domain-tenant and CAE fixes' tests.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: `run_auth_code_flow` calls `open_system_browser` unconditionally (mod.rs:263) and binds its own private listener (:221-228), so `sign_in`, `consent_for_scopes` and `reauthenticate` have no test; the test module covers only silent paths, `authorize_url` shape and `ensure_same_identity` in isolation (:1027-1061). Untested branches listed (nonce mismatch :294-296, tid check :313-318, missing tid/oid :306-321, `known_tenants` re-insert :671-673) are real. A launcher seam is the smallest change that unlocks them, and it is a prerequisite for testing fixes to findings 0 and 2.

findings.title: Zeroize discipline is one-sided: the load path is meticulous, but the freshly issued refresh token, the raw /token body and the PKCE verifier are dropped un-wiped
findings.rationale: `load_refresh_token` (token_cache.rs:303-373) documents at length why every chunk is wiped and returns `Zeroizing<String>`, `AccessToken` zeroizes on drop, and `Debug` redacts — but on every refresh the NEW refresh token (`TokenResponse.refresh_token: Option<String>`) is dropped as a plain `String` at the end of the `spawn_blocking` closure, the entire response body containing all three tokens sits in `bytes` and is freed un-wiped, and `serde_json` builds intermediate `String`s for each field. `oauth2-5.0.0/src/types.rs` has no `zeroize`, so the `Zeroizing` copy of the verifier leaves the original in place. Either the heap-wipe property matters (then these leaks defeat it on every refresh) or it does not (then the load-path ceremony is misleading). DEVELOPMENT.md:342-345 presents zeroize-on-drop as an invariant reviewers check.
findings.proposal: Make `TokenResponse.refresh_token`/`access_token`/`id_token` `Zeroizing<String>` (serde supports `Zeroizing<T>` via `#[serde(deserialize_with)]` or a small newtype), wrap `bytes` in `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` (`bytes.to_vec()` then zeroize; or read into a `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` via `chunk()`), and drop the theatre around the PKCE verifier (either generate the verifier locally with `Zeroizing` + `Sha256` or accept the copy and remove the misleading wrapper). Small, mechanical; add a doc line in DEVELOPMENT.md listing exactly which buffers are wiped so the claim matches the code.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: wire.rs:14-23 `TokenResponse` fields are plain `String`; mod.rs:167/200 hold the full body as `Bytes` un-wiped; mod.rs:455-457 moves `refresh: String` into the `spawn_blocking` closure and drops it un-zeroized; `id_token` is dropped un-wiped. oauth2 5.0.0 in the registry has no `zeroize` dependency (checked Cargo.toml/src/types.rs), so the `Zeroizing` copy at mod.rs:280-281 leaves the original verifier in place. One nuance: `access_token` is moved into `AccessToken` (mod.rs:461-465), which zeroizes on drop (token_cache.rs:101-105), so only refresh/id tokens, the body bytes and the verifier are the gap. DEVELOPMENT.md:340-343 does present zeroize-on-drop as a review invariant. Low is right.

findings.title: Two keyring deletes run inline on the tokio runtime (sign_out and the InvalidGrant purge) and take the std `CHUNK_SET_LOCK` on a worker thread, contrary to the documented spawn_blocking rule
findings.rationale: Save and load were moved to `spawn_blocking` precisely because Credential Manager / Secret Service calls block and the chunk loop makes N of them (plus one probe). `delete_chunks` does the same loop, and `delete_refresh_token` blocks on `CHUNK_SET_LOCK` — a std mutex that a `spawn_blocking` writer may be holding for the duration of its own keyring round trips. Doing that from `access_token_inner` (which also holds the per-scope async refresh lock) or `sign_out` parks a tokio worker for the whole time; on Linux the first call may also block on D-Bus connection setup inside `ensure_keyring_store`. Not a correctness bug today, but it is the pattern the crate's own comments say not to write.
findings.proposal: Add `async fn delete_refresh_token_blocking(tenant, oid)` (or reuse the `spawn_blocking` shape in `store_token_outcome`) and use it at both sites; in the purge arm, `spawn_blocking` and ignore the join result as today. Consider a `repo_invariants` source-scan test that every `save_/load_/delete_refresh_token(` call outside `token_cache.rs` sits inside `spawn_blocking`.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: mod.rs:535 (InvalidGrant arm, while holding the per-scope async refresh lock) and mod.rs:564 (`sign_out`) call `delete_refresh_token` inline inside `async fn`; token_cache.rs:376-380 takes the std `CHUNK_SET_LOCK` and loops keyring syscalls (delete_chunks :385-396), and `ensure_keyring_store` may do D-Bus setup on first call. The crate's own doc (mod.rs:440-444, 501-506) says these go through `spawn_blocking`. Cleanup, low.

findings.title: InvalidGrant purge is unconditional, so a refresh still in flight across a completed reauthenticate can delete the new refresh token (narrow window)
findings.rationale: Refresh locks are per `(tenant, scope_key)` by design, so two audiences refresh concurrently with the same RT. If refresh A (say ARM, on a slow link) is in flight when the session is re-established — `reauthenticate` or `consent_for_scopes` stores RT2 and re-inserts `known_tenants` — and A then returns `invalid_grant` for RT1, the arm deletes RT2 and removes the tenant: the operator who just completed a browser round trip is immediately "signed out" again and the reauth toast reappears. The window is a few seconds around every reauth, and the readiness fan-out (six concurrent refreshes) plus a 30 s HTTP timeout make it reachable. The purge should be conditional on the keyring still holding the token that failed.
findings.proposal: Keep a monotonically increasing `session_generation: AtomicU64` bumped by `store_token_outcome`; capture it before `post_token` in `access_token_inner` and skip the purge (return `RefreshTokenMissing` without deleting/removing) when the generation changed — or compare the loaded RT to the stored one under `CHUNK_SET_LOCK` before deleting (`delete_refresh_token_if_eq`). Test: with a wiremock delay on one scope set, complete a `reauthenticate`-shaped store during the delay, then assert the keyring still holds RT2 and `known_tenants` is intact after the delayed `invalid_grant`.
findings.verifier_notes: Logic verified: mod.rs:507-513 loads RT1 under the per-scope lock, :527-538 deletes whatever the keyring holds and removes the tenant on `InvalidGrant`, and `reauthenticate` (:661-673) stores RT2 and re-inserts the tenant with no generation check. But the rationale overstates reachability: for the race the failing `/token` POST must stay in flight for the entire browser round trip (seconds to tens of seconds) after the sibling refresh already purged and the operator completed reauth — realistic only with a badly stalled connection near the 30 s timeout, not 'a few seconds around every reauth'. The generation-counter fix is cheap and reasonable; low.

findings.title: `token_adapter::token_error` duplicates the `From<AuthError> for UiError` code table by hand with a 'must match' comment but no test pinning agreement
findings.rationale: `grep -rn "token_error(" apps/desktop/src-tauri` finds only the definition — no test exercises it. AGENTS.md calls this function "the sole mapping" at the `BearerProvider` boundary and the repo has invested a whole module (`core::reauth`) in preventing exactly this kind of two-table drift for the fatal codes; the third code (`consent_required`) and any future one are still a hand-copied pair. A variant renamed or added on the dto side (e.g. the `InteractionRequired` proposal) would compile here and silently fall to `token_error`.
findings.proposal: Either derive: `TokenError::new(UiError::from(err).code, ..)` if the dependency direction allows (src-tauri already depends on dto), collapsing the duplicate; or add a unit test in `token_adapter.rs` iterating the same constructible `AuthError` cases as `auth_error_maps_to_stable_code_and_retryable` and asserting `token_error(e).code == UiError::from(e).code` for the classified variants and `"token_error"` for the rest.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: token_adapter.rs:21-29 hand-copies the code table with a 'must match' comment; there are no tests in token_adapter.rs and no repo_invariants test names it (fanout.rs:110 only mentions the code). `reauth_agreement_tests` in dto/lib.rs pins UiError vs TokenError predicates, not this mapping. Deriving is feasible: src-tauri's `crate::dto` re-exports `azapptoolkit_dto::UiError` (dto.rs:5), so `let ui = UiError::from(err); TokenError::new(ui.code, ui.message)` collapses the duplicate. Low.

findings.title: Rule 13 emits the broad-prefix delegated advisory for declared scopes regardless of consent; the group blurb and predicate doc promise admin-consented ones
findings.rationale: For an app-registration row `scope_values` is the manifest's declared delegated scopes, and `rule_high_risk_delegated` never consults `perms.has_admin_consent`. Since the rule was widened to the broad-prefix predicate (`Mail.`, `Files.`, `Group.`, `Sites.`, `Directory.`…), every app that merely declares a user-consent `Mail.Read` or `Files.Read` delegated scope now lands in the "High-risk delegated permissions" group whose blurb says "Admin-consented delegated scopes". Delegated access under user consent is confined to the consenting user, so the group misleads the operator and buries the genuinely admin-consented cases. The only Rule 13 test (tests.rs:394-415) exercises just the two exact entries plus `User.Read`, so the broad-prefix behaviour under `score_application` is unpinned.
findings.proposal: Thread the per-client AllPrincipals scope set the runner already keeps (audit.rs:914-931, `delegated_scopes_by_client`) into app rows too, so the rule can tell an admin-consented scope from a merely declared, user-consentable one; keep the two PS entries unconditional; emit the broad-prefix half only for consented scopes, or word it separately ("declared" vs "admin-consented"). Do NOT gate on the coarse `has_admin_consent` flag alone: the grants read is best-effort (audit.rs:933-939) and a failed read would silently hide the advisory, against the over-report-is-safe stance at permissions.rs:194-197. Fix groups.rs:113 to match whatever the rule actually reports, and add the table rows.
findings.verifier_notes: Premise verified: scoring.rs:480-484 filters `perms.scope_values` with `is_risky_delegated_scope` and never reads `has_admin_consent`; for app rows `scope_values` is the declared manifest (audit.rs:1475); permissions.rs:167-169 says "when admin-consented"; groups.rs:113 blurb says "Admin-consented delegated scopes"; the widening comment at scoring.rs:471-479 and CHANGELOG-archive:377-381 frame the change around admin-consented scopes; the only Rule-13 table (tests.rs:399-403) has three rows. Overstated: for SP rows `scope_values` IS the AllPrincipals grant set (audit.rs:1264-1267), so the blurb is right there; and the proposed `has_admin_consent` gate is app-level, not per-scope, and fails silent when the tenant-wide grants read fails. Advisory only (no score), so medium is for group noise/mislabeling, not ranking.

findings.title: `Calendars.ReadWrite` keeps its PS-ported medium weight while the net-new `Contacts.ReadWrite` is high — reconcile or document the exception
findings.rationale: The file states the weighting rule explicitly and applies it to Mail, Contacts, MailboxSettings, Chat, Device, Notes and Files — but `Calendars.ReadWrite` (write to every calendar in every mailbox, its own comment says) stays at 5 points while `Contacts.ReadWrite` earns 10. An app with org-wide calendar write ranks Low (5 < RISK_MEDIUM=8) while the same reach on contacts ranks Medium. No test guards the write-half placement; `mailbox_family_risk_entries_agree_with_the_scoping_role_map` only checks spelling.
findings.proposal: Make the decision explicit: either promote `Calendars.ReadWrite` to HIGH with a CHANGELOG note (ranking shift), or add a comment at permissions.rs:145 saying the medium placement is deliberate PS parity (`Constants.ps1:123-130`) and why. A guard test asserting every mailbox-family `*.ReadWrite` in `graph_mail_role` is HIGH would fail today, so it needs the same `INTENTIONALLY_*` exemption pattern the file already uses (permissions.rs:660-668).
findings.verifier_notes: Inconsistency is real: permissions.rs:105-108 states write=high/read=medium, MailboxSettings.ReadWrite (113) and Contacts.ReadWrite (123) are HIGH, Calendars.ReadWrite (145) is MEDIUM; `mailbox_family_risk_entries_agree_with_the_scoping_role_map` (602-637) only checks spelling. But it is not a bug: the medium list "Mirrors Constants.ps1:123-130" (129-130), the entry's own comment says it sat there "for its whole life" (137-145), CHANGELOG-archive:366-375 fixed only the plural typo and kept the tier, and mod.rs:3-6 says every constant matches the legacy module. The write=high sentence at 105-108 describes how the *net-new* additions were weighted. So this is a PS-parity vs net-new consistency question — a risk-model call, not a defect.

findings.title: Read halves of several high-weighted families score zero (Contacts.Read, MailboxSettings.Read, Device.Read.All, Notes.Read.All, Application.Read.All)
findings.evidence:
permissions.rs SUBSUMED table (narrower side only, none in either risk table):
313:    ("MailboxSettings.Read", &["MailboxSettings.ReadWrite"]),
319:    ("Contacts.Read", &["Contacts.ReadWrite"]),
375:        "Device.Read.All",
383:        "Application.Read.All",
405:    ("Notes.Read.All", &["Notes.ReadWrite.All"]),

MEDIUM table (lines 132-157) contains `Mail.Read`, `Files.Read.All`, `Sites.Read.All`, `Chat.Read.All`, `Calendars.Read` — but not the five above.

permissions.rs:672-676 (test scope):
    /// scans table -> role map ... It cannot catch an entry that was never written
    fn every_broader_subsuming_permission_carries_a_risk_weight()  — walks only `broaders`.
findings.rationale: `Contacts.Read` is a Graph mailbox-family permission `graph_mail_role` maps (scoping.rs:88), so Rule 11 raises "Organization-wide mailbox access: Contacts.Read" for it — yet it contributes 0 points while `Calendars.Read` (same family, same reach class) contributes 5. `MailboxSettings.Read` reads every mailbox's forwarding/auto-reply settings; `Device.Read.All` and `Application.Read.All` are tenant-wide directory reads on par with `Group.Read.All` (medium). The existing guard test deliberately checks only the broader side of the subsumption table, so these narrower-side omissions are invisible.
findings.proposal: Add `Contacts.Read`, `MailboxSettings.Read`, `Device.Read.All`, `Notes.Read.All` (and decide on `Application.Read.All`) to `MEDIUM_RISK_APP_PERMISSIONS`, with a CHANGELOG note. Extend the guard test with a narrower-side walk for the mailbox family: every value `graph_mail_role` maps must be in HIGH or MEDIUM, or be listed in an `INTENTIONALLY_UNSCORED` table with a reason (`Mail.ReadBasic*` would be the documented exceptions).
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: MEDIUM list (permissions.rs:131-157) contains Mail.Read, Files.Read.All, Sites.Read.All, User/Group.Read.All, Directory.Read.All, Chat.Read.All, Calendars.Read — not Contacts.Read, MailboxSettings.Read, Device.Read.All, Notes.Read.All, Application.Read.All (nor GroupMember.Read.All / RoleManagement.Read.Directory). The comment at 153-156 says the read halves of "the two families added" were weighted, but CHANGELOG-archive:48-60 lists five new HIGH families (MailboxSettings, GroupMember, Chat, Device, Contacts, Notes) and only Chat/Calendars got read halves. `Contacts.Read` is mapped by `graph_mail_role` (scoping.rs:87) so Rule 11 raises ORG_WIDE_MAILBOX for it while it adds 0 points, versus 5 for `Calendars.Read`. `every_broader_subsuming_permission_carries_a_risk_weight` (656-695) walks only the broader side. Ranking impact is real (org-wide Contacts.Read + MailboxSettings.Read = Low). Needs a CHANGELOG note per AGENTS.md; `Mail.ReadBasic*`/`Calendars.ReadBasic` are natural INTENTIONALLY_UNSCORED entries.

findings.title: Rule 7 labels multi-year certificates as "Long-lived secrets" and the dated-certificate path is unpinned
findings.rationale: `all_creds` chains secrets and certificates, so a standard 2-year PKI certificate scores +3 under an issue literally titled "Long-lived secrets". Rule 17 tells the operator to replace secrets with certificates; doing so with a normal certificate lifetime raises the app's score and files a misnamed finding. The constant is documented as `LONG_LIVED_SECRET_DAYS` (Credential-Analysis.ps1:169) — a secret threshold. The only certificate test (`certificates_do_not_trip_long_lived_when_no_dates`, tests.rs:1933) covers the no-dates case; nothing pins that a dated long-lived certificate is flagged, so narrowing the rule breaks no test.
findings.proposal: At minimum, word the issue by kind ("Long-lived credentials" or separate secret/certificate lines) and add table rows for a 400-day certificate and a 400-day secret so the behaviour is pinned either way. Treat exempting certificates or giving them a longer threshold as an explicit risk-model decision (CHANGELOG note; PS parity per mod.rs:3-6 cannot be checked in-repo) rather than a bug fix — long certificate lifetimes are also a legitimate rotation finding.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: `is_long_lived` is kind-agnostic (credentials.rs:104-109), `all_creds` chains secrets and certificates (scoring.rs:896, 928-932), issue text is "Long-lived secrets (>1 year)" (191), the only certificate test is the no-dates case (tests.rs:1933-1944), and `rich_app`/`long_lived_secret_adds_three` use PasswordCredential only. The Rule-17 tension is real. Overstated: nothing shows the legacy rule excluded certificates (the cited `Credential-Analysis.ps1:169` is unverifiable — see finding 14), so "bug" and "medium" are too strong; the certain defect is the misnomer plus the unpinned path.

findings.title: Three emitted issue markers have no finding group or posture count, so unconfinable org-wide reach is scored but invisible in the workbench
findings.evidence:
types.rs:558-563 (module doc of `issue`):
/// Stable markers the UI keys audit facets/home cards off. The scorer emits
/// issues that **start with** these ... the frontend matches the same constants ...
types.rs:576, 588, 606: UNSCOPABLE_LEGACY_MAILBOX / UNCONFINABLE_MAILBOX / UNCONFINABLE_SHAREPOINT

apps/desktop/web-rs/src/views/audit_view/filter.rs:61-95 `issue_marker` keys: high_risk_perms, high_risk_delegated, external_exposure, orgwide_mailbox, scoped_mailbox, legacy_mailbox_scope, orgwide_sharepoint, redundant_perms, scoped_sites, ownership — none for the three above.
apps/desktop/web-rs/src/views/audit_view/groups.rs:47-136 GROUP_CATALOG: same key set.
Only consumer: row.rs:65-66 (tab routing).
findings.rationale: An app holding `Contacts.Read` on Office 365 Exchange Online (score 0, `is_unscopable_legacy_exchange_permission` true) or `Sites.Manage.All` on Office 365 SharePoint Online (score 0) gets a scorer finding that reaches every mailbox/site, yet appears in no findings group, no posture count and no filter — it is only discoverable by reading the issues column in the All-apps pane or the export. The scorer deliberately keeps these out of `orgwide_mailbox`/`orgwide_sharepoint` so they carry no Fix, which is correct, but the workbench then has no advisory home for them. This is the same shape as `high_risk_perms` (Actionable, no bulk fix).
findings.proposal: Add an advisory group (e.g. key `unconfinable_reach`, title "Org-wide reach the toolkit cannot confine") in `GROUP_CATALOG` + `issue_marker`, matching the three markers with `starts_with`, no remediation kinds, tab "permissions"; count it in `posture_counts`. On the core side, add the three markers to `emitted_issue_markers_are_stable` so the doc claim "asserts the scorer still emits each" becomes true.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: filter.rs:60-96 `issue_marker` and groups.rs:46-138 GROUP_CATALOG have no key for UNSCOPABLE_LEGACY_MAILBOX / UNCONFINABLE_MAILBOX / UNCONFINABLE_SHAREPOINT (types.rs:574, 585, 604); posture.rs:31-70 has no count; row.rs:65-66 tab routing is the only frontend consumer. The catalog's own stated principle supports the fix: "Advisory groups (no group-level fix) still render — visibility with an Open deep-link beats hiding a finding the audit scored" (groups.rs:43-45), and `group_remediation_kinds` already returns `&[]` for unknown keys (269-279). Mitigation the finding omits: the app Permissions tab and held-permissions panel do show a callout for the legacy grants (CHANGELOG-archive:1297-1312, exchange-scoping.md:130) — but nothing in the workbench findings/posture does. `emitted_issue_markers_are_stable` (tests.rs:594-684) indeed omits these three; other tests cover them (tests.rs:155-161, 1028, 1076-1087), so the doc claim at types.rs:562-563 is loosely true across the file, not for that one test.

findings.title: Bare-value `least_privilege_alternative` assumes Graph, and the permission picker calls it while holding the resource id
findings.rationale: The picker is the "full live catalog (every resource)" per the architecture doc, so an operator selecting the Office 365 Exchange Online `Mail.Read` appRole sees "Org-wide — tenant-wide reach. Scope to specific mailboxes (Exchange RBAC)." — advice the toolkit's own `is_scopable_exchange_resource_permission` says cannot be applied on that resource. AGENTS.md says the value-only scopable forms are pinned out; this Graph-defaulting wrapper is the one remaining value-only entry point, and its sole caller has the resource in scope two lines above.
findings.proposal: Remove `least_privilege_alternative` from `mod.rs` re-exports (or mark `#[deprecated]`), change `scope_hint(resource_app_id: &str, value: &str)` to call `least_privilege_alternative_for(Some(resource), value)`, and add the bare-value name to the repo_invariants source scan that pins the other deleted value-only helpers.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: `least_privilege_alternative(value)` hard-codes Graph (permissions.rs:250-252); its only non-test caller is `scope_hint(value: &str)` (permission_picker.rs:259, 285), invoked at 448 with `resource_app_id` cloned two lines earlier (442); the picker has a resource selector (62, 141) so Office 365 Exchange Online appRoles do reach it and get the RBAC pointer that `is_scopable_exchange_resource_permission` (scoping.rs:126-131) says cannot apply. Not pinned: the GONE list in repo_invariants/commands.rs:131-135 covers only the three deleted mailbox gates. Note `scope_hint` also uses value-only `is_sharepoint_orgwide` at 288, and `downgrade_hint`/`app_permission_risk_badge` are value-only by documented design (permissions.rs:193-197); the unit test at permissions.rs:564-584 uses the bare form and would move to `_for`.

findings.title: Covered narrower permissions keep their own weight (surface-area model) — pinned by test but not stated in the architecture doc
findings.rationale: `deduped()` exists because scoring a duplicate grant twice let identical effective access rank differently. A fully-covered narrower Graph permission is the same situation one step removed: `Mail.ReadWrite`+`Mail.Read` (15, High) has exactly the reach of `Mail.ReadWrite` alone (10, Medium), and `Directory.ReadWrite.All` + `User.Read.All` + `Group.Read.All` scores 20 vs 10. Rule 18 already computes the covered set. This is a risk-model judgment (surface area vs. reach), but today it is neither scored-as-reach nor documented as intentional.
findings.proposal: Option (b): add one sentence to the Rule 18 section of audit-findings-and-remediation.md stating that a covered narrower grant keeps its Rule 1/2 weight (surface area, and PS parity), pointing at `redundant_permissions_rule_is_advisory_with_remediation`. Option (a) would break rule-for-rule PS parity (mod.rs:3-6) and the characterization snapshot (tests.rs:1345), so it is a risk-model change, not a cleanup.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: scoring.rs:56-92 scores every grant; tests.rs:1551-1565 pins 15 for Mail.ReadWrite+Mail.Read with the comment "redundancy itself adds nothing"; the doc says Rule 18 is "advisory, no score (the broader permission already carries the risk weight)" (audit-findings-and-remediation.md:209-213). So "neither scored-as-reach nor documented as intentional" is overstated: the current behaviour is pinned and half-documented; what is missing is the explicit sentence that narrower grants keep their weight. The `deduped()` analogy (types.rs:293-298) is about the same (resource,value) pair listed twice — identical access — not about distinct permissions.

findings.title: `deduped()` clones grants, scopes and `mail_scopes` per scored principal — measurable but negligible at current throughput
findings.rationale: Per scored principal this performs 2×|grants| + |scopes| String clones for set keys, clones every grant and scope again for the output, and deep-clones the `HashMap<String, MailPermissionScope>` (which itself holds `Option<String>` scope names/filters). `redundant_app_permissions` in the same module already shows the borrowed pattern (`HashSet<(&str, &str)>`). The bench in CHANGELOG-archive (193k apps/s) shows scoring is not the bottleneck, so this is polish, but it is the one avoidable allocation cluster in the 10k-app loop.
findings.proposal: Polish only: borrowed keys `HashSet<(Option<&str>, &str)>` for the dedup sets, or have `score_one`/the SP phase pass `AppPermissions` by value (audit.rs:1593 and 1286 do not reuse `perms` afterwards) so the dedup can run in place. Not worth a signature change on its own; do it when touching the code.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified types.rs:310-332 (2×|grants|+|scopes| String clones for set keys, full clone of grants/scopes, `mail_scopes.clone()`), called at scoring.rs:882 and 1052. But the finding's own numbers undercut its framing: 193k apps/s (CHANGELOG-archive:1187) means ~50 ms of scoring for 10k apps, and the `format!`-built issue/recommendation Strings per rule dominate allocations, so "the one avoidable allocation cluster" is overstated.

findings.title: Five in-code docs have drifted from the code after the resource-aware refactors
findings.evidence:
scoring.rs:403-407:
/// Takes the resource-stripped values: SharePoint scoping is encoded by the
/// permission name alone, so unlike the mailbox rule it needs no resource.
fn rule_sharepoint_advisory(perms: &AppPermissions) -> ...   // gates on Graph resource at 416-420

types.rs:334-338: "/// ... Resolved once per scoring pass and threaded through, rather than re-derived per rule.\n    pub fn app_role_values(&self)"  — scorer no longer calls it (only src-tauri/commands/audit.rs:1523).

scoring.rs:1043: "/// nor fix. `perms.app_role_values` are the SP's *granted* app roles" — the field is `app_role_grants`.

types.rs:345-373: the `is_scoped` doc ("True when `grant` is a mail permission ... **Gated on the grant's own resource first.**") runs straight into "True when **every** grant carrying `value`..." and attaches to `value_fully_scoped` at 362; `is_scoped` at 373 has no doc.

permissions.rs:94-101: the "Net-new ... the EWS `full_access_as_app` scope" comment sits above `"MailboxSettings.ReadWrite"` (113); the entry it describes is `crate::scoping::EWS_FULL_ACCESS_AS_APP` at 126.
findings.rationale: These are the docs an agent is told to read before editing the subsystem; each now states the opposite of the code (resource-stripped vs resource-gated), names a method that is not the field, or documents the wrong function. The `is_scoped` fusion is the most likely to mislead: its resource-gate explanation is the load-bearing invariant AGENTS.md cites.
findings.proposal: Fix the `rule_sharepoint_advisory` doc to say it takes the grants and gates on Graph; rewrite `app_role_values`'s doc to say it serves the runner's Exchange probe only (or move it to the runner); change `perms.app_role_values` → `perms.app_role_grants` in the SP doc; insert a blank `///`-free line so `is_scoped` keeps its own doc; move the EWS comment down to line 126.
findings.verifier_notes: All five drifts verified. findings.title: AuditItem boundary note says the whole payload is snake_case, but RiskLevel / CredentialStatus / CredentialKind serialize PascalCase
findings.rationale: The note is the wire-format contract AGENTS.md points to ("a rename is a wire-format change"). A reader trusting it would expect `risk_level: "critical"` in the JSON export / cached runs and could 'normalize' the enums to snake_case — which would break every cached `AuditRunResult` and external consumer of the JSON export. Three casings coexist in the same payload (snake_case kinds, PascalCase levels/statuses, lowercase list status).
findings.proposal: Amend the note: field names are snake_case; `RemediationKind`/`AuditPrincipalKind`/`ScopeMechanism`/`MailPermissionScope` are snake_case values; `RiskLevel`/`CredentialStatus`/`CredentialKind` are PascalCase variant names and must stay so. Optionally add a serde round-trip test that pins `"Critical"` and `"ExpiringSoon"` literals.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified types.rs:510-512. `RiskLevel` (14-20), `CredentialStatus` (45-51) and `CredentialKind` (130-134) derive Serialize with no rename, so they serialize as "Critical", "ExpiringSoon", "Certificate". The note is wrong a second way the finding missed: its parenthetical "no serde rename on ... nested remediation/scope types" contradicts `RemediationKind` (403-404), `AuditPrincipalKind` (480-481), `ScopeMechanism` (160-161) and `MailPermissionScope` (179-180), which all carry `rename_all = "snake_case"`. No test pins the PascalCase literals (grep for "\"Critical\"" finds only UI labels). Minor overstatement: `ListCredentialStatus` (71-78) is not part of `AuditItem`, so the payload has two casings, not three.

findings.title: `AuditItem.publisher` is overloaded: publisher domain for app rows, home-tenant GUID for SP rows

scoring.rs:1028-1030:

scoring.rs:1093:        publisher: sp.app_owner_organization_id.clone(),

findings.title: `credential_status` day-bucketing is re-implemented in `sso_cert_status`; the expired-certificate keyId helper lives in the command layer
findings.evidence:
credentials.rs:77-84 (private):
fn credential_status(days: Option<i64>) -> CredentialStatus {
    match days {
        None => CredentialStatus::Unknown,

        Some(d) if d <= EXPIRY_WARNING_DAYS => CredentialStatus::ExpiringSoon,

apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/sso/mod.rs:1119-1124 (byte-identical arms).

apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/remediation.rs:35-41:
fn expired_cert_key_ids(app: &Application, now: DateTime<Utc>) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut ids: Vec<String> = app.key_credentials.iter().filter(|c| is_expired(c.end_date_time, now))...

findings.title: Rule 19 wording claims Entra-tenant reach for a personal-accounts-only audience
findings.rationale: `PersonalMicrosoftAccount` means Microsoft accounts only — no other Entra directory can consent to the app — but the issue text tells the operator it "can be consented to from any Entra tenant and personal Microsoft accounts", and the recommendation to set `AzureADMyOrg` is not a valid transition for an MSA-only app. The test table (tests.rs:433-500) has no `PersonalMicrosoftAccount` row.
findings.proposal: Give `PersonalMicrosoftAccount` its own arm with reach text "personal Microsoft accounts" (keep the score, since credentials/permissions are still reachable outside the directory) and a recommendation that fits; add the row to `external_exposure_scores_only_reachable_multitenant_apps`.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified scoring.rs:596-602 folds `PersonalMicrosoftAccount` into `(true, true)` and 608-612 then reports "any Entra tenant and personal Microsoft accounts"; the table at tests.rs:435-486 has no `PersonalMicrosoftAccount` row. Microsoft's manifest reference defines that value as "Personal Microsoft accounts only" (no other Entra directory can consent), so the reach text is wrong for it while the marker "reaches outside this tenant" (types.rs:616) and the score stay defensible. The claim that `AzureADMyOrg` is "not a valid transition" is unverified — Microsoft's howto-modify-supported-accounts page lists all four values as settable via the manifest — so the recommendation part is a wording nit rather than an error.

findings.title: The module's PowerShell provenance contract is unverifiable in-repo and no rule catalog exists
